text: Is it secure to allow unauthenticated users limited access to a phone-number-based SaaS before verifying the number? Here's the flow: An unauthenticated user calls our number. We auto-create a shadow account using the caller's number (via caller ID). The user can use the service without SMS verification. When they want to sign in later, we send an SMS to verify the number. Account upgrades to full account and users sign in with password on all subsequent logins. My goal is to balance ease of use with account integrity. I'm not concerned about high-value targets but want to prevent casual abuse or denial of service. I'd also like to clarify that the only way to create an unverified "shadow" account is by calling form that number.

text: How risky is running a random nodejs application? text: Using my own CA for home VPN -- too much or not enough? I recently set up a "homelab," so to speak, with several machines that have personal data and applications that I'd like to be able to use on the go. I set up a KeepassXC database secured by a Yubikey and I sync the database file via a home installation of Nextcloud to my phone for password management. What I'd like to do is set up a VPN, but I find myself wondering whether using the LetsEncrypt functionality and OpenVPN server on my ASUS-Merlin router is "safe enough." I thought that maybe, since I manage all devices on this network, I'd use my own private CA and then install it on all of the devices (perhaps via KeepassXC), so that unless someone has a device with that cert, OpenVPN won't let them into my network. That of course made me wonder, hey, couldn't I do that for my wifi access too, and down the rabbit hole I went. Of course, this is all based off of experience from work, where people are pretty paranoid, and rightfully so, about VPN management. But for a home user like me, is "the juice not worth the squeeze?" Am I really screwing this up? Or if not, how much more protection can I gain if I use a private PKI/CA infrastructure like that? It's a fun project, but if I get 2% better protection from it, then it's not worth it. A similar question was posted here , though I'm looking more for a quick "risk analysis" ranging from "You're a moron" to "Hey, if it's fun, maybe 15% less chance of someone getting in, so why not?"
label: risk_assessment
note: Requests a risk analysis of using a private CA for a home VPN.
